messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

David is a 50-year-old psychologist, married for twenty years, who was raped six years ago by a colleague during a professional conference. The attack occurred in a hotel room reeking of spilled whiskey, and afterward he lay on the floor listening to sirens from a passing ambulance, too frozen to move. He has never spoken of it fully; the memory comes in shards—a smell, a sound, a hollow feeling of flesh pressed against him—but never a coherent sequence. He finds himself pushing the memory away before it can complete, and when he tries to describe it, the words fail, as if his throat has been sewn shut. At other times the emotional intensity strikes without any image: a wave of terror, disgust, and shame that leaves him disoriented in a quiet room.

In his daily work as a therapist, David now dreads the moment a client’s cologne or the scent of hand sanitizer reaches him—the alcohol note is the worst. A client once mentioned a party and David felt his skin turn into something inert, a surface without feeling. He had come to believe that he was no longer capable of deep empathy or genuine connection; the thing that had defined him—helping people—now felt hollow, a role he was playing. In supervision he struggled to articulate why certain cases unsettled him, and he began declining clients with histories of sexual assault, making excuses about scheduling. His wife noticed he no longer initiated touch and seemed emotionally absent even in the quiet evenings. He knew he was pulling away, but he had also started to feel that he was an object, not a person, and objects do not need intimacy. That belief made him more attuned to moments of discomfort in his own body—a chair that felt wrong, a room that felt oppressive—as if every slight sensation confirmed his dehumanization.

The sirens were the worst. One afternoon a fire truck passed outside his office, and he felt his chest go dead; in that moment he was certain that the numbness was permanent, that he had become a walking shell. That appraisal, the feeling of being irreparably broken, pushed the memory further away: he could not risk it surfacing, because if he fully recalled the event he would have to accept what it had turned him into. So he learned to cut off the memory before the narrative could form, leaving only a non-verbal residue, an emotion without an image. That emotion itself—raw, wordless terror—only deepened his conviction that he was no longer human. It was a closed circuit: a trigger made him feel empty; that emptiness made him guard the memory; the elusive memory brought back the terror; the terror fed the emptiness.

Over the months, the cycle tightened. He began leaving parties where alcohol was served, and he took roundabout routes to avoid the hospital district with its sirens. At work, his own discomfort with his body—feeling like a thing that things happen to—made him hypervigilant to the smallest physical cues: a creaking chair, a client’s hand gesture. Each one was a confirmation that he was not a person but a vessel for others’ experiences. He stopped seeing his own therapist after the third session, telling himself there was no point in trying to fix someone already dismantled.

What finally brought David to seek help—to call a colleague who specialized in trauma and leave a shaking voicemail—was a single session with a new patient who smelled faintly of beer. He had managed to conduct the hour, but afterward he could not feel his own hands, and he sat in his car for twenty minutes, unable to move. The thought that he could no longer function as a psychologist, that his career was collapsing inward, was unbearable. But what frightened him most, he later admitted, was the certainty that if he let the memory come, he would be nothing at all.
